form: Keywords: Athabaskan, language contact, Nicola Dene, Nɬeʔkepmxcín.

In 1895, as Franz Boas was putting his small collection of Nicola Dene (Athabaskan) lexical data into print (Boas 1895; reprinted 1924), Father J.M.R. Le Jeune published a similar but distinct vocabulary in his mimeographed southern BC missionary newspaper (Kamloops Wawa 1895; mentioned in passing by Wyatt 1998:222). 2 Taking up just a paragraph, this hitherto unstudied contribution was modest. But in proportion to the limited information available on Nicola, which seems already to have had only rememberers (cf. Knab 1980), not speakers, the potential for a useful contribution was high. In this study I compare Le Jeune’s piece with Boas’, noting two insights that emerge to the benefit and detriment of Nicola studies. Because “not all the Nicola material has been brought together” (Bakker and Grant 1996:1129), I further point out probable Nicola words in other sources, not previously collected into the small literature on this language.
2 The good news: Le Jeune’s contribution
First, the good news: Kamloops Wawa (1895) increases our knowledge of Nicola lexicon by at least 10% (and additional sources still further). We quote in full for the background information supplied:

Le Jeune’s position as a missionary is no doubt what induced him to comment on the “paganism” of these men. He was an Oblate Catholic priest, known for his unusual ability to communicate well in, among others, the four Interior Salish languages spoken in his district: Nɬeʔkepmxcín (Thompson), Nsyilxcən (Okanagan), Secwepemctsín (Shuswap) and St’át’imcets (Lillooet) (Blake 2014). In that capacity, he enjoyed a close, trusting and ongoing relationship with various important local people. Notably for our purposes, these included both Charley -Alexis Mayoos — the first Indigenous literate in, and the popularizer of, the Chinuk pipa script Le Jeune introduced — and the well-regarded Chief Celestin a.k.a. John/Johnny Chilihitsa of Nicola Lake (cf. Robertson 2014 s.v. Nikola.) These factors suggest the possibility that Le Jeune may have personally elicited his Nicola data, whether in person or from a local Aboriginal person’s notes in Chinuk pipa, which was the first literacy of many hundreds of aboriginal people. The wordlist that follows Le Jeune’s prefatory remarks is certainly not his own, however. He must have been double -checking the same quite limited lexicon that made its way into Boas’ paper from the field work of James A. Teit, George M. Dawson, and J.W. Mackay (Boas 1895:36). Contact between missionary-linguists and anthropologist-linguists would not be a rare occurrence in the Pacific Northwest (Tomalin 2011:151ff). It is known that Le Jeune and Teit, for example, communicated. There is even a friendl y letter in Nɬeʔkepmxcín Salish (!) from Teit to the priest preserved in the National Archives of Canada (Teit 1893; Robertson 2004:217-220). And Le Jeune had recently met Boas in person and been exposed to the latter’s desire and methodology for ethnographic data collection (Rohner 1969:138; Kamloops Wawa #123, December 1894). form: In summary, Le Jeune managed to expand the known Nicola lexicon as summarized in Boas (1895) by three phrases, a not inconsiderable increase of about 10% over the roughly 31 previously known items.9 More good news emerges from linguists' sporadic observations on Salish -Nicola interaction. Nɬeʔképmx speakers borrowed from “Athapaskan” — certainly from the Nicola enclave — into Nɬeʔkepmxcín, e.g. petə́le(ʔ) ‘blood’ (cf. Thompson & Thompson 1996:232). Nearby St̓át̓imcets got k̓ʷúnaʔ 'salmon eggs, salmon roe' (V an Eijk 2013:226) as “probably a borrowing from Athabaskan q̓u·nʔ 'roe' (Krauss 1985:485), with now extinct Nicola being the most likely source”. Kuipers (2002:158) dates this loan as early as Proto-Interior-Salish, giving *ʔak̓ʷn/l 'fish roe' and comparing it with Carrier ʔək̓un 'fish eggs' from Nater (1977:58). It is interesting to compare the data from the printed sources here referred to with what Harrington elicited from rememberers (1941). But since “Teit found the last person who could speak the language properly had died about 1890” (Wyatt 1998:220, citing Boas regarding a late female elder, 1895:552), little is added by Harrington’s consultants to the picture I have sketched. One additional word putatively of Nicola emerges from these people’s memories, <aik> 'kinnikinnick', cf. / ʔéyk in Nɬeʔkepmxcín Salish (Thompson and Thompson 1996:7); this is not noted by the latter as a loan but it is certainly noncognate with e.g. neighbouring St’át’imcets Salish km̓us (Van Eijk 2013:180) and Nsyilxcən skulís (Somday 1980:631).

form: Two further strands of research promise to identify even more Nicola lexemes. There are a number of reputedly Dene place names in the former Nicola territory of north-central Washington (Wyatt 1998:221, citing Bouchard and Kennedy 1984 [not yet seen by m e]). And the ethnonyms for the Nicola in neighbouring Salish are built on roots apparently lacking Salish cognates: s- /twíx=mxʷ in Nɬeʔkepmxcín, s-/mələ́q=amxʷ in Nsyilxcən, and ɬu•/ɬwák=amxʷ in Secwepemctsín (Wyatt 1998:222).

form: Now the bad news: quite strong and well -entrenched lexical influence from (L2?) Nɬeʔkepmxcín Salish looks likely in moribund Nicola. (The only study to have noted this, in passing and without substantiation, is Bakker and Grant 1996:1129.) A general consequence of this is to complicate the already vexed question of Nicola’s place in the Dene fa mily tree (Kinkade et al. 1998:49 -51, 67, Wyatt 1998:220).

Several of the items listed in (1) -(3) are obviously cognate with words of other Dene languages. Harrington concludes that the Nicolas were a Tsilhqut'in (Chilcotin) remnant (1943). But a Dene language that is equally geographically close and is better documented is Dakelh (Carrier), which likewise borders Salish to the north (Walker 1998:2). form: But the Salishanist examining Le Jeune’s testimony of Nicola Dene will perceive many sequences that more closely resemble morphemes of Salish. Two languages of that family are spoken in “the Nicola”, as the region is locally called: Nɬeʔkepmxcín and Nsyilxcən (Wyatt 1998:221). The latter is the latecomer (Boas 1895:553), and I will show by footnotes to selected morphemes below that the Salish -looking items below bear a greater resemblance to Nɬeʔkepmxcín.

form: The main published Nɬeʔkepmxcín source (Thompson and Thompson 1996), while it catalogs virtually all documented inflectional forms of each root, explicitly omits personal names for reasons of cultural sensitivity (p.xxiii), so these proposed etymologies are hard to test. But all three of these names can be plausibly interpreted with Salish meanings, albeit with root-derivations that are otherwise unattested in the dictionary. If these have no Dene etymologies, they support the hypothesis that the Nicola people were culturally Salishanized. That claim is reported as fact by Teit (1900-1921, quoted in Wyatt 1998) and is implicit in Le Jeune’s words above. None of this, however, strongly suggests a linguistic shift to Salish.

form: The morphological makeup of this item, elicited by Teit (Boas 1895:36), may be compared with that of modern Nɬeʔkepmxcín / ɬəq’=á[•q’]n’ek ‘small silvery fish with many fins, resembling herring or sardine (used as bait for sturgeon); brassy minnow? ?Hybognathus hankinsoni’ (Thompson and Thompson 1996:152). Factoring out the DIMINUTIVE exponences in that word, that is the posttonic reduplication of q’ and the suprasegmental glottality on n’ (Thompson and Thompson 1992:89), we get the root /ɬəq’ ‘wide-flat’ (Thompson and Thompson 1996:152) with the lexical suffix that is underlyingly =éne(ʔ)k ‘belly’ (p.537). 23 It is conceivable that the initial t of (6) is a typographical error for a “barred l”, ɬ, leading to a nearly perfect match with the 1996 form. Here Teit’s gloss is interesting: ‘a small fish called eyi΄nik in Thompson’. That Salish form, while not to be found in the 1996 dictionary, is apparently based on the root /y’eh ~ /y’e ~ /y’ ‘good’ (Thompson and Thompson 1996:450) and certainly shares the lexical suffix =ének with /ɬəq’=á[•q’]n’ek. Thus it may mean literally ‘good belly’. (The vowel a results from the influence of the nearby uvular q, Thompson and Thompson 1992:17.) The possibility cannot be ruled out that there once existed in Nɬeʔkepmxcín —at least as used by L1 Nicola speakers — an otherwise unattested form like **/ɬəq’=ének=cn24 with an additional lexical suffix as shown in (7). Certainly more than one lexical suffix can easily occur on a word, as in modern /mn=uʔs=áqs ~‘[a] saw’ and n-/wəx̣́=enk=éks-e-s ‘to take [something] out of [someone’s] hand’.

form: The cited word for ‘nearby’ is in fact used in Nɬeʔkepmxcín to exhort the addressee to move closer, as in néʔe xeʔ mèɬ (e /míceʔq uxw) ‘(you sit) right here!’ (Thompson and Thompson 1996:389). Because it was Teit — a Nɬeʔkepmxcín -speaker and married into the Nɬeʔképmx community—who collected (12), it can be assumed that he would have recognized and noted any obviously Nɬeʔkepmxcín material. So while this and other items above may have their ultimate sources in that Salish language, their pronunciation and their morphological treatment by Nicola Dene people suggest nonnative usage. This could include either a distinct L2 variety of Nɬeʔkepmxcín or else old borrowings into Nicola. Teit concluded that “the Nicola had a long local history” and close associations with Nɬeʔképmx speakers (Wyatt 1998:220).

Summarizing from the limited evidence, it is clear that the Nicolas experienced bilingualism in the unrelated Nɬeʔkepmxcín. There is evidence too that the historical shift from Nicola to that language was drawn -out, accompanied by phonological and morphological distortions that possibly engendered a distinct L2 version of it. This inferred scenario of language death corresponds to Thomason and Kaufman's contact outcome of “shift with normal transmission” of the target language [TL] (1988:110ff).

The question is to what extent Nicola “interfered”, that is altered any of the structural domains, in the Salish TL, an influence which should correlate with relative sizes of speaker populations, speed of shift, and group cohesion and isolation (pp. 119 -120). It is predicted that a relatively small shifting group, shifting to the TL over several generations, will generally acquire it without significant interference from their (former) language (pp. 50, 119ff). We know the Nicolas to have become gradually outnumbered by the Salish starting shortly before White contact (Wyatt 1998:221), thus generally matching the conditions for perfect acquisition. That is in fact a typical result of North American indigenous language shift to the dominant English (Thomason and Kaufman 1988:121).

But partway into the process, the outnumbering of the Nicolas accelerated suddenly with the Salish acquisition of horse culture, though the Nicolas nonetheless retained a conscious separate identity well after White contact (Wyatt ibid.). This latter consi deration likely set the stage for a somewhat greater Nicola imprint on their variety of Nɬeʔkepmxcín ; the apparent structural distortions of Salish seen above would then constitute the predicted slight (Thomason and Kaufman 1988:121-129) or moderate interference (pp. 129ff).

As for the degree or course of structural erosion in the ancestral Dene language, we can say little since we neither have nor can reconstruct usable phonological or morphosyntactic data (cf. Krauss 2005:115).

I have shown that Le Jeune (Kamloops Wawa 1895) added a statistically significant amount of new data to the known lexicon of Nicola Dene. However, that lexicon was so sparse in any case that his data may not resolve any of the outstanding questions about Nicola.

form: But I have expanded on Teit's hunch (in Boas 1895) that certain items in Nicola are of Nɬeʔkepmxcín Salish origin, by identifying several more candidates for etymologies specifically from Nɬeʔkepmxcín (and not Nsyilxcən, the other neighbouring Salish language). Their frequency (perhaps seven of 34 data points; Golla estimates “a fe w dozen” known Nicola lexemes, 2011:319) in turn may help explain the difficulty in assigning Nicola a place in the Dene family (about which cf. Krauss 2005:115). Expanded as they may be, however, the data on this geographically isolated Dene language remain scant and, as I show, must be handled with the Salishanist’s caveats here conveyed.
